canonicalQuestion: How do I ask AI a question so it gives me a useful answer?
aliases: How do I write a better prompt?
How can I get a more useful answer from AI?
answer:
Give the AI a proper brief. “Make this better” leaves it guessing what better means to you: shorter, clearer, friendlier, or finally something your boss will read.

Your prompt—the instructions and information you give it—should name the job, the useful background and what you want back. Clear instructions and relevant examples help steer the response.

For example, instead of “write an email,” try:

“Help me explain our new vacation policy to employees who have not read it. Write a friendly email under 250 words. Include the effective date and where to ask questions. Do not invent details; ask me for anything you need.”

You can reuse that structure: help me do [job], for [audience], using [relevant context], in [format]. Include [must-haves] and avoid [unwanted material].

Then read what comes back. If it misses, give it a specific correction: “You assumed a start date. Leave a placeholder,” or “The main point is buried. Put it first.” You are directing the draft, not searching for magic words.

Keep confidential, personal and workplace details out unless you know you have permission and understand the tool’s handling of them. A useful brief does not need to contain every detail you know.

canonicalQuestion: My boss wants a weekly project update. How can AI help me prepare it without sharing confidential information?
aliases: How can AI help me structure a weekly project update without sharing confidential details?
answer:
Use AI to build the structure, then add and check the real project facts in your company’s approved document system. That gives you a useful starting point without sending confidential information to AI.

Start with a tool your employer permits. Some tools can work inside a document: Microsoft’s current Copilot in Word guidance describes drafting from an outline or reference files, then revising the draft. Availability depends on your subscription and organization’s settings. Being able to attach a file does not mean that file is permitted—use only material approved for that tool.

For an update that keeps project facts out of AI, give it safe context: who will read the update, what they need from it and how long it should be. For example: “My manager needs a short weekly update showing progress and decisions needed. Create a blank format under 200 words with questions to help me fill it in. Leave project facts as placeholders.” If you have a blank company template that is approved for sharing, use it as a reference.

Inspect the structure before filling it in. Does it make room for a delay, its consequence and the help you need? If not, ask for that specific change. Then add this week’s facts yourself in the approved work document. Keep confidential notes outside AI; changing names alone may still leave identifying details.

Before sending, compare every date, number, status and commitment with your records. Check what was left out, too: “on track” could mislead your manager if it depends on an approval that has not arrived. AI can help find gaps when you are allowed to share the material, but its reassurance is not independent verification.

Save the empty format and useful instructions for next week. Replace the facts and check them again. Reusing the structure saves work; carrying forward an old deadline creates new work.

canonicalQuestion: Why does AI sometimes give me a confident answer that is wrong?
aliases: Why should I verify an AI answer even when it sounds certain?
Why can AI sound confident and still be wrong?
answer:
Because sounding convincing and checking a fact are different jobs. A language model—the part of an AI system that generates text—can produce a plausible answer without having reliable evidence for it.

Training teaches it patterns in language. Those patterns help it construct a response, but they do not guarantee that a particular date, name or claim is true. A plausible but false statement is often called a hallucination.

An OpenAI research paper gives a revealing example: several models supplied polished answers about a researcher’s dissertation, yet got its title and year wrong. The answer had the shape of a fact; it was still false.

The paper also explains why uncertainty can turn into confident guessing: if training or tests reward a correct guess but give no credit for “I don’t know,” guessing can score better. That helps explain the behaviour; it does not mean every error has the same cause.

When a claim matters, ask for its original source, open it and check whether it supports that exact claim. Asking “Are you sure?” may produce another confident paragraph. What you need is evidence you can inspect.

canonicalQuestion: What information is safe to put into ChatGPT or another AI tool?
aliases: What should I avoid sharing with an AI tool?
answer:
A conservative starting point is public material or an invented example that contains no sensitive information. Being able to paste something into an AI tool does not mean you have permission to share it there.

For workplace material, check your employer’s policy and which tool and information it permits. For personal material, consider whose information it is and whether sharing it could expose them. Privacy settings do not grant someone else’s permission.

Keep passwords, access codes, account details, private records and confidential company or customer information out of a general AI prompt. Review the whole attachment, including comments, hidden notes and details visible in screenshots.

Removing names is not enough by itself. A job title, small town and unusual event may identify a person when combined. If you cannot confidently separate the sensitive details, use an invented example or ask for a blank template instead.

For example: “Show me a friendly reminder email about an overdue invoice, using invented details.” Add the real customer and invoice information later in your approved work system.

Share only what the task needs. If permission or the tool’s current handling of your information is unclear, leave the information out.
